angle: Why did a painter who had sworn loyalty to the French king paint the French army's darkest night?
answer: When the French fled in 1814, everyone who had served them faced a loyalty inquiry, so Goya asked the new government to fund paintings of the 1808 uprising; but instead of a victory he painted a nameless queue of executions, the first war painting with no heroes.
logline: Goya swore loyalty to Joseph Bonaparte, kept his court post and took the king's medal, but by 1814 the French had fled and collaborators faced inquiries, so Goya asked to paint the uprising, but he painted no victory, only faceless rifles, a lantern and a man with wounded palms, but at his feet lies the man shot a moment before, so his proof of loyalty became a picture of war with no heroes, only a queue.
hooks: This painting was Goya's way of proving he wasn't a traitor.
The man who painted this had worked for Napoleon's brother.

script.text: So Goya asked the new government to fund paintings of the uprising.

script.text: The soldiers have no faces, only a wall of backs and rifles.
The only light is a lantern on the ground.
It falls on a man with raised arms and Christ's wounds in his palms.
But at his feet lies the man shot just before, arms flung the same way.
Behind him, the next men wait, covering their eyes.
So his proof of loyalty became war with no heroes, only a queue.
Manet later borrowed its firing squad to shoot an emperor.

post.caption:
Goya had sworn loyalty to Napoleon's brother. When the French fled, he asked to paint this, and the 'proof of loyalty' turned out to be a picture of war with no heroes at all.
Patriot or survivor: what was Goya?
